lessons.title: WAEC Structure: Complete the Sentence by Reading Its Pattern

description.text: Use the words around a blank to identify the structure, form and meaning the sentence requires.

lessons.subject: english-language

objectives.statement: Identify the phrase pattern and word class required by a sentence.
Choose a grammatical form that agrees with tense, comparison, number or the sentence ending.

text.text: John should be through with his work, ______? The answer is not chosen by sound alone. The completed sentence must have the correct question tag and must preserve the meaning of should be through.

Structure questions test relationships inside the sentence. First identify what comes before and after the blank. Then ask whether the blank needs a verb form, modifier, determiner, preposition, conjunction or tag. Finally check tense, number, comparison and meaning. Do not select an option because it is common in isolation.

items.text: Read the sentence without the options.
Name the pattern: question tag, comparison, adverbial phrase, plural form or clause link.
Test each option in the full sentence.
Read it aloud once for grammar and once for meaning.

prompt.text: Complete: John should be through with his work, _____?

steps.description: The clause is positive and its auxiliary is should.
A positive statement takes a negative question tag.

steps.expression: John should be through, shouldn't he?
steps.description: The pronoun matches John and the tag keeps should.

answer.text: Shouldn't he? is correct: it reverses the polarity and matches the auxiliary and subject.

text.text: WAEC structure options often differ by one small form. Identify the pattern before looking for the familiar-looking word.

points.text: Name the structure required by the blank.
Check form, agreement, tense and meaning together.

prompt.text: The footballers have been practising _____. Which completion fits the structure?

feedback.text: The present perfect continuous verb phrase is complete; the blank naturally takes an adverb describing how they practise.

hint.text: What kind of word can describe practising?

prompt.text: James appears _____ wiser than his friends.

feedback.text: Much can modify the comparative adjective wiser. Many modifies countable nouns, while more wiser and most wiser create incorrect comparison forms.

hint.text: Wiser is already comparative; choose its suitable intensifier.

summary.text: Structure is the relationship between words in the complete sentence.

lessons.title: WAEC Lexis: Field, Collocation and Register

description.text: Choose vocabulary that belongs to the subject field, combines naturally and suits the situation.

lessons.subject: english-language

objectives.statement: Use surrounding subject matter to narrow a vocabulary choice.
Choose a word that forms a natural collocation and appropriate register.

text.text: The bank granted the trader a _____ after reviewing the security. A loan, a crop or a melody could fit another sentence, but the finance field and the verb granted narrow the answer.

WAEC lexis is not a dictionary race. Read the field—law, agriculture, health, government, science, transport or finance—then check the words that naturally occur together. Collocation is the normal partnership between words; register is whether the expression suits a formal report, conversation, advertisement or technical setting.

rows: What subject or activity is being discussed?
Would this expression suit this reader and situation?
content.alt: Three filters for WAEC vocabulary choices.

prompt.text: The bank granted the trader a _____ after reviewing the security: loan, harvest, sermon or engine.

steps.description: The field is finance and lending.
Loan is the natural collocation with granted and security.
The other options belong to different fields and do not fit the verb.

answer.text: Loan is correct because it fits the finance field and the collocation granted a loan.

content.title: Related is not the same as suitable

text.text: An option may belong to the same broad topic but still form the wrong partnership. Test the word in the complete sentence.

points.text: Check normal word partnerships and register.

prompt.text: Which phrase is the natural formal collocation?

feedback.text: Conduct an investigation is the conventional formal collocation. The other options are nonstandard or use the wrong word form.

hint.text: Which verb normally partners with investigation in formal English?

prompt.text: A sentence about irrigation, seedlings and harvest belongs chiefly to which field?

feedback.text: Irrigation, seedlings and harvest are agricultural vocabulary clues.

summary.text: WAEC vocabulary is learned through use, field and collocation—not isolated lists.

description.text: Use phonemic contrasts and spelling traps to recognise vowels, consonants and stress patterns.

objectives.statement: Distinguish pure vowels, diphthongs and common consonant contrasts.
Recognise the stressed syllable or word in a spoken contrast.

text.text: The words blood and flood rhyme, but their vowel is not the long sound suggested by oo. Oral English asks what is pronounced: sound, stress and contrast—not what the spelling appears to promise.

Use a phonemic chart as a map. A pure vowel stays at one mouth position; a diphthong glides between positions. For consonants, compare voicing and place of articulation. For stress, say each word naturally and identify the syllable that receives the strongest beat. These methods work even when the spelling is irregular.

prompt.text: Which is a pure vowel: /aɪ/, /aʊ/, /iː/ or /ɔɪ/?

steps.description: Each diphthong moves from one vowel quality to another.
The sound keeps one main quality, so it is a pure vowel.
Choose by sound type, not by the number of letters used to spell a word.

answer.text: /iː/ is a pure vowel; the other three are diphthongs.

text.text: Say the pair, identify the symbol or stress pattern, then say it again in a sentence. Recognition and production strengthen each other.

points.text: Use phonemic contrasts and stressed syllables as evidence.

prompt.text: Which word has the same vowel sound as seat?

feedback.text: Seat and seed share /iː/. Sit, said and site contain different vowel sounds.

hint.text: Say each word; ignore the spelling similarity of site.

prompt.text: In the noun record, which syllable receives the main stress?

feedback.text: The noun record is normally stressed on the first syllable; the verb record shifts stress to the second.

hint.text: Compare noun REcord with verb reCORD.

summary.text: Oral English is a system of sound contrasts, not a spelling quiz.
